summary: POC scoping to define latency SLOs (TTFT vs TPOT), mapping to traffic slices, sizing assumptions, and a measurement plan. Customer emphasized p95 and p99 bounds for both first token and per-token costs in chat and batch generation. Agreed actions: share benchmark artifacts, provide traces, and schedule infra setup call.
topics: TTFT vs TPOT definition and trade-offs
Traffic decomposition (short chat vs long generative jobs)
p95/p99 target setting and risk envelopes
Measurement plan: sampling, warmups, KV cache hit assumptions
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick roll call — maya from Redwood here, Ethan from SE, and...
[00:12] Leah Kim: Leah here, hi.
[00:15] Marco Silva: Marco — afternoon.
[00:18] Priya Nair: Priya, SRE.
[00:20] Jonas Reed: Jonas, product.
[00:22] Maya Patel: Awesome. Goal for today is to scope the POC: define success criteria, how we measure TTFT (time-to-first-token) vs TPOT (total-per-token), target p95/p99 bounds, and get a traffic sampling plan. We'll also map who needs to provide logs and timing. Sound good?
[00:35] Leah Kim: Yes, that's what we need. We're trying to validate whether Redwood Dedicated or Private will meet our latency goals before committing. Our main worry is tail latency when people do long multi-turn medical summaries.
[00:48] Ethan Ross: Great, can you describe your traffic shape? average prompt size, distribution of short chat vs long generation?
[00:55] Marco Silva: Rough numbers: about 65% short chats (2-6 turns, avg 40 tokens output), 25% medium (single-turn summaries ~200 tokens), 10% long generative jobs (500-2k tokens, usually batch). Peak qps is around 80 reqs/s, 95th around 150 during busy periods.
[01:18] Maya Patel: That's helpful. For SLOs, do you care primarily about first-response latency for interactive chat (TTFT), or total completion time for long jobs (TPOT)?
[01:26] Leah Kim: Both. For chat we need first token to be under 300ms p95 ideally, p99 < 700ms. For long jobs we measure TPOT — we want median to be reasonable and p95/p99 to not blow out; target p95 for TPOT is 4-6s for 200-token jobs, p99 maybe up to 12s. Those are aspirational.
[01:40] Ethan Ross: Ok that maps to two separate SLOs. One note—TTFT is sensitive to batching and prefix caching; TPOT is heavily influenced by throughputs and per-token compute. We'll need to instrument both separately.
[01:54] Priya Nair: Also, our compliance team wants audit logs for every request and KMS integration for key material if we do Private. That influences timeline.
[02:02] Maya Patel: Understood. We'll include security checklist in the next steps.
[02:06] Jonas Reed: Timeline check — we want a go/no-go decision in 6 weeks. Is that feasible?
[02:11] Ethan Ross: Yes, typical pilot is 4-8 weeks depending on trace availability and infra access. With your traces we can do a baseline within a week, then run controlled sweeps.
[02:20] Maya Patel: Let's talk measurement plan. Our template separates sample collection, warmup, and measurement sweeps. Marco, can you send anonymized request traces with timestamps, prompt + response lengths, and session IDs? We don't need PII.
[02:33] Marco Silva: We'll extract and scrub — probably 7 days. There might be some noisy internal traffic; we can flag that.
[02:40] Ethan Ross: For TTFT we'll define traffic slices: interactive short-chat (40 tok), medium-summary (200 tok), long-generate (1k tok). For each slice we measure p50/p95/p99 for TTFT and TPOT. We'll run boxcar sweeps at target QPS and burst profiles.
[02:55] Leah Kim: How do we handle cache warmups and KV cache behavior? Our live app uses heavy caching for recent sessions.
[03:02] Ethan Ross: Good question — we'll simulate a cold-start phase and a warm cache phase. In Dedicated/Private you can pin session caches, but in hosted there are more eviction dynamics. We'll record cache-hit-rate assumptions and run both extremes.
[03:16] Priya Nair: Will you include GPU utilization and queuing metrics? We need stress points to understand scaling costs.
[03:21] Maya Patel: Absolutely — our runtime emits per-GPU util, queue depth, batch size distribution, and token/sec. We'll capture those in the benchmark artifact.
[03:30] Jonas Reed: On targets, Leah asked p95 300ms for TTFT. That's tight; do you think that's realistic for our model family?
[03:36] Ethan Ross: Depends on model and quantization. If you're on a small 7B-ish model and using INT8 with an optimized kernel, TTFT 300ms p95 is achievable for single-turn short chat at modest QPS with prefix cache. For larger models or higher concurrency it gets harder.
[03:50] Maya Patel: We should capture two SLO tiers for the POC: conservative (what we expect now) and stretch (what you want). That makes the POC actionable.
[03:58] Leah Kim: For conservative let's say TTFT p95 450ms, p99 1.2s; TPOT for 200-token p95 8s, p99 20s. Stretch is the 300ms/700ms and 4-12s you mentioned.
[04:12] Ethan Ross: Perfect. We'll baseline against conservative and show delta for optimizations (caching, batching, quant).
[04:18] Maya Patel: Ok, sample sizes — to reliably estimate p99 we need enough data. We'll run each sweep until we gather at least 10k requests per slice or 1 hour, whichever comes first. That's in the runbook.
[04:32] Marco Silva: 10k sounds fine. For the long jobs, that might mean multiple parallel runs.
[04:36] Ethan Ross: Right, for long generative jobs we do smaller QPS but sustained to accumulate samples.
[04:41] Leah Kim: Any tests around multi-tenant noise? We run multiple customers on our platform; noisy neighbor risk is real.
[04:46] Maya Patel: In Dedicated you'll have isolated pools; in hosted we can schedule tests on a reserved pool to emulate noisy neighbors. We'll run a 'noisy neighbor' sweep where we inject bursty synthetic jobs and observe tail effects.
[04:58] Jonas Reed: Costs — can you estimate the expected token cost delta between configurations? We need to show Opex impact.
[05:03] Ethan Ross: We'll produce a cost model: tokens per request * model cost per token + GPU hours for peak. The Optimize toolkit will recommend batching/quantization to lower per-token cost, we'll show trade-offs with latency.
[05:15] Priya Nair: Security question again: If we go Private, what's the timeline for KMS/HSM integration?
[05:20] Maya Patel: Typically 2-3 weeks to validate KMS keys and peering after infra access. We'll document exact steps in security doc we'll send.
[05:27] Leah Kim: Great. Can you outline a concise acceptance criteria for the POC?
[05:31] Maya Patel: Yes. Proposed POC acceptance criteria: 1) TTFT: conservative p95 met for short-chat slice; 2) TPOT: conservative p95 met for 200-token slice; 3) No unbounded p99 tail during noisy neighbor sweep; 4) Metrics and dashboards instrumented and reviewed; 5) Security checklist signed off.
[05:47] Marco Silva: And also cost projection within 20% of our internal goal.
[05:50] Maya Patel: Add that as item 6.
[05:53] Ethan Ross: Measurement specifics — we'll run three phases: baseline on your current infra (if you provide traces we'll replay to your current infra), Redwood-hosted pilot runs with identical traffic slices, and stress/scale tests to hit peak QPS and bursts. For each run we produce TTFT/TPOT histograms, per-GPU utilization, batch size distributions, and a small csv of timed samples.
[06:16] Leah Kim: For histograms, do you capture percentiles with confidence intervals?
[06:19] Ethan Ross: Yes, we provide bootstrapped CI for p95/p99 estimates so you know sample uncertainty.
[06:25] Jonas Reed: Risk register — what are the top risks?
[06:28] Maya Patel: Quick list: missing or low-quality traces, infra access delays, data residency approvals, model mismatch (your prod model differs from test model), and unexpected burst patterns. We'll include mitigation steps.
[06:40] Priya Nair: On infra access, we prefer not to give full creds; we'll use read-only S3 + VPC peering.
[06:46] Maya Patel: Works for us. We'll provide a minimal checklist.
[06:49] Marco Silva: For the measurement harness, any preference on the replay tool? We use a homegrown replayer but can export to the Redwood sampler format.
[06:56] Ethan Ross: We accept either. If you can export as timestamped requests in JSONL we can plug it in. We'll send schema.
[07:03] Leah Kim: Ok, what's the expected schedule if we start now?
[07:07] Maya Patel: Week 1: traces and template exchange, baseline replay; Week 2: Redwood-hosted sweeps and initial tuning; Week 3: scale & noisy neighbor tests; Week 4: final report and handoff. That fits a 4-week core run, with extra 2 weeks for security/ent signoffs if needed.
[07:23] Jonas Reed: Good — aim for go/no-go by 6 weeks then.
[07:26] Maya Patel: Any other questions?
[07:28] Marco Silva: One small thing—how do you measure streaming tokens for chat? Do you treat token arrival intervals as part of TTFT?
[07:33] Ethan Ross: We define TTFT as time from request arrival to the first token emitted. Streaming inter-token timing is measured separately as token throughput; TPOT includes the full time until final token. We'll include both metrics.
[07:44] Leah Kim: Perfect.
[07:46] Maya Patel: Alright, recap of next steps: Maya/Ethan send benchmark template + replay schema, Marco provides traces, Priya confirms peering constraints, we schedule infra call. We'll target the benchmark template out by Friday (2026-05-07).
[07:58] Jonas Reed: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[08:00] Maya Patel: Thanks — we'll follow up with calendar invites and the artifacts.

Notes on transcript quality: occasional mis-heard acronyms (K-V catche in raw transcript), filler words and slight crosstalk.
